meeting_header:
Date: 2026-11-18 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Location: Zoom | Meeting ID: ff-20261118-seastone-001
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Carlos Mendes, Aisha Rahman, Devon Park, Lina Ortiz (Seastone)
summary: Initial discovery to understand Seastone's private deployment constraints: strict egress controls for maritime data, region-locking for EU/UK customers, preference for VPC peering via transit gateway, and SOC2/KMS requirements. Agreed to share diagrams and schedule deeper network dive.
transcript:
00:00 Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then Priya will kick into the network questions.
00:10 Carlos (Seastone): Hey, thanks — Carlos here. We'll try to keep this tight, we have some legacy egress policies that are... um, yeah.
00:22 Priya (Redwood SE): Great, I'll start with high level: are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private for the pilot?
00:30 Aisha (Seastone): Private. We can't allow unmanaged egress from our VPCs; all outbound must go through our egress proxy or approved NATs. Also, data for our EU customers must never leave eu-west-1 and must be encrypted with our KMS.
00:48 Jordan: Got it. So primary constraints are egress control, region residency, and KMS integration. Is that correct?
00:55 Carlos: Yes and we also need audit logs for model invocations — long retention, at least a year.
01:05 Priya: We can support private deployments with a VPC-based control plane. Two common patterns: private endpoints (interface endpoints) inside your VPC, or full VPC peering/transit gateway to Redwood-managed subnets. Which is closer to your network ops preference?
01:25 Devon (Seastone): Transit gateway peering is preferred. We run a central transit for all customer infra so putting Redwood behind that is easier for routing and monitoring.
01:33 Priya: Cool. A few clarifying Qs: do you require us to terminate TLS inside your VPC or is mutual TLS to Redwood acceptable?
01:42 Aisha: We need keys to be customer-managed. Prefer CMKs in our KMS. If Redwood can use customer KMS for at-rest encryption and not exfiltrate keys, that's mandatory.
01:55 Jordan: We have integrations for customer KMS via key wrapping and HSM in some private deployments. We'll get details in the security pack.
02:05 Lina (Seastone): Another constraint: our egress to the internet is tightly scoped; anything that attempts to dial out to third-party endpoints is blocked except approved CDNs. Do Redwood nodes ever reach out to model repos or S3 for fetching weights at runtime?
02:22 Priya: For private deployments, model artifacts are typically pre-staged in the customer's environment or in Redwood-managed object storage that we can place in the same region. For hosted variants there's external pulls, but for private we avoid outbound fetches at runtime — we stage.
02:34 Carlos: Okay good. About regions — we have EU customers plus some UK-specific contracts. Is it possible to pin the deployment to eu-west-1 only?
02:45 Priya: Yes, you can pin model serving to a single region. We recommend colocating the private control plane in your region as well. A caveat: if you want high availability across multiple AZs in the region, that's standard, but crossing regions would require replication and has legal implications.
03:02 Devon: We also need to ensure traffic egress IPs are static for firewall allow-lists. Can Redwood provide fixed egress IPs when using private endpoints?
03:13 Priya: With a dedicated network path via transit gateway, egress IPs are your VPC SNAT or NAT gateway — Redwood won't introduce dynamic outbound IPs. For hosted boxes, we provide ranges but they aren't suitable for strict allow-lists.
03:27 Carlos: So we should set up private endpoints + TGW attachment, and manage the NAT/eProxy on our side?
03:34 Priya: That's the cleanest. Redwood will accept inbound connections from your VPC to our private endpoints, and you control outbound.
03:42 Aisha: What about audit logs — invocation traces, prompts, and response metadata. Can Redwood write logs into our logging sink (S3 or GCS) for retention?
03:52 Jordan: Yes, for private deployments we can push invocation logs to a customer-controlled bucket via a connector. We need to discuss PII filtering — many customers want structured events not the raw prompt.
04:06 Aisha: We'll want both structured events and the raw text kept in a separate, encrypted bucket with strict ACLs. Also SOC2 is a checkbox for us; do you have certs and can you supply the report?
04:18 Jordan: Redwood is SOC2-compliant; we can provide an attestation and will include it in the security package. For private deployments, a lot of controls are implemented in your environment — we'll document separation of duties.
04:30 Devon: One think — latency. Our use cases are near-real-time routing decisions for vessels, so tail latency matters. If we colocate in eu-west-1 and keep requests local, what's typical p50/p95 for a 128-token generation?
04:45 Priya: On our optimized rigs with quantized models for that size, p50 is typically 40-80ms, p95 is 120-250ms — depends on batching and KV cache hits. For private we can tune the instance type and batching to hit your SLOs.
04:58 Lina: Are there options for burst capacity if we get seasonal spikes?
05:03 Priya: Yes, we can provision burst pools or allow cross-region fallback, but cross-region fallback would violate your region residency constraint, so bursts have to be in-region. We can do autoscaling with reserved capacity set aside for the pilot.
05:20 Carlos: Pricing question quickly: dedicated pools vs private — major difference?
05:25 Jordan: Dedicated reserved capacity is about guaranteed throughput and simpler billing; private adds more integration work and licensing. We'll send a pricing comparison.
05:33 Aisha: Do you support SSO and RBAC integration with our IAM?
05:36 Jordan: Yes SAML SSO and role mappings; for private deployments you can map to your identity provider and enforce RBAC at the control plane.
05:45 Devon: Network nit: what BGP or route exchange do you expect on TGW? We typically propagate route tables centrally, do you want static routes or full propagation?
05:56 Priya: We typically request route propagation with specific route tables per attachment, and we can accept either static or propagated — we'll share the recommended route table layout in the template.
06:10 Carlos: Any blockers we should know about from infra side?
06:14 Priya: The common ones: nonstandard CIDR ranges that overlap with Redwood-managed ranges (we'll check), strict egress that prevents staging model artifacts, and KMS policies that prevent cross-account access.
06:26 Aisha: On KMS, our policy won't allow key material to leave account; if Redwood requires cross-account encrypt/decrypt, that's a no-go.
06:34 Jordan: Understood — we can do an architecture where keys never leave your account; Redwood will call a customer-side decryption proxy or use envelope keys. We'll include options in the security pack.
06:48 Lina: About pilot scope — we want a 6-week pilot, start with 2 models, 3 qps sustained with 50qps burst, and retention of logs for 12 months. Is that realistic?
07:01 Priya: That sizing is small and straightforward. We'll propose instance types and a cost estimate. For 50 qps bursts, reserve some burst capacity in pool or use cold-scaling fast warmup.
07:12 Carlos: Okay, that's helpful. Anything else on networking?
07:15 Devon: One more: egress to house internal monitoring — do you need outbound to Datadog or will we host the agent?
07:22 Priya: We prefer customers host the telemetry agent in their VPC and forward to Datadog; we can also push metrics to your Prometheus endpoint if you expose it.
07:31 Jordan: Quick recap and next steps: Redwood will share private deployment checklist, security pack, and pricing; Seastone will share VPC diagram and egress policy; schedule network deep-dive.
07:45 Aisha: Sounds good.
07:47 Carlos: Thanks.
07:49 Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts by Monday.
07:53 [call ends — 48:10 recorded total] 

Notes on transcription: occasional overlaps, some model names mis-transcribed in parts of the recording (e.g., 'quantize' heard as 'quant eyes'). Where timestamps are approximate, speakers may talk over one another during clarifying Qs.
